newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Range trading 'till Wed.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Range trading 'till Wed.

text.p: If the U.S. Treasury market had its way, Tuesday would probably not exist so it would not have to wait so long for the July retail sales report, due on Wednesday.
Since the wish won't come true, market participants said Treasuries will likely just stick to narrow ranges, paying only scant attention to Tuesday's handful of economic data.
"We are just going to be marking time until Wednesday," said Michelle Laughlin, chief Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities Inc.
"Everyone is waiting to see how retail sales look," she added.

Still, players said Tuesday's data would garner some attention, especially the weekly chain store sales numbers. Sales in July were far and away above expecations. Thus, the weekly data could provide clues to the extent of the strength, and whether it was induced by warm weather.
At 0900 EDT/1300 GMT, the BTM-Schroders version will be released, followed at 1455 EDT by the Johnson Redbook report.

At 0830 EDT, second-quarter productivity/unit labor costs data are due. Productivity was expected to have risen 0.7 percent in the second quarter after a 2.6 percent gain in the first quarter, according to a Reuters poll.
Unit labor costs were seen up 2.7 percent compared with 2.5 percent.
Ahead of the retail sales numbers on Wednesday, the data were expected to get a muted response. But some noted that a low productivity number could spook the market.

Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, said a weak productivity number would not only bother those looking for strong productivity to continue, it could damage "Brave New World" thinking that high productivity would keep inflation low.
The one caveat, players said, is that many believe the productivity data are unreliable.
Also Tuesday, both the Atlanta and Richmond Feds will release regional economic activity for July at 1000 EDT.
In late trading on Monday, the 30-year bond rose 1/32 to 96-21/32 to yield 6.63 percent, on a late-day short-covering rally.
